title: DeepMind quietly disbands the AlphaFold team as scientists move to Gemini
subtitle: The Nobel-winning group behind protein structure prediction has been dissolved over the past year, with most authors reassigned to Gemini and a quarter of the original team having left Google entirely.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Financial Times reported on July 29 — and Google DeepMind subsequently confirmed — that the dedicated AlphaFold team has been dissolved. Most of the authors of the original AlphaFold papers have been reassigned over the past 12 months, primarily to Gemini-related projects and to a smaller set of scientific efforts covering enzyme design, nuclear fusion, and genomics. Nobel laureate John Jumper left DeepMind in June for Anthropic, and two of his AlphaFold colleagues followed him. Almost a quarter of the full-time Google DeepMind authors of the original AlphaFold papers have now left the company.

The restructuring is not the end of AlphaFold as a product. The database of 200 million structure predictions is still online, AlphaFold 3 remains available for academic use, and the AlphaFold Server continues to operate. What has changed is that AlphaFold is no longer a first-class research program with its own team, roadmap, and headcount. It has become a service backed by an on-call rotation. That is a specific institutional shift — the kind that happens when a research bet has fully paid off and the parent org decides the marginal researcher is worth more embedded in the current flagship than kept together in the group that made the prior breakthrough.

The move fits a larger pattern in 2026. DeepMind has been consolidating around Gemini as its central AI system since the Gemini-Genesis merger of research leadership in Q1. Meta dissolved its FAIR research org into product teams last fall. OpenAI shut down its Superalignment team in 2024 after Ilya Sutskever's departure. The economic logic is consistent — as base models get better, they absorb more specialized scientific work as a downstream capability rather than a separate program. The counter-argument, which the AlphaFold departures make loudly, is that the specialists who made the breakthrough do not necessarily want to be absorbed, and losing them has costs that do not show up on a headcount spreadsheet.

For learners: this is a reminder that AI research careers now bifurcate quickly. If you are a scientist whose work sits inside a large lab's flagship, you have leverage — and if that flagship pivots, your options are to move with it, move to a competitor (in Jumper's case, Anthropic), or start something small and focused. The AlphaFold-to-Anthropic pipeline is worth watching; it suggests the frontier labs still see scientific AI as an attractive place to compete, even as the lab that pioneered it moves on.
